newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish economy boom seen boosting credit growth.
newsitem.headline: Irish economy boom seen boosting credit growth.

text.p: Ireland's booming economy is expected to underpin a strong growth trend in Irish credit once again when the central bank releases statistics for end-December on Thursday, economists believe.
The degree to which the consumer boom will boost the credit figure is a bone of contention, however.
Some economists believe that as the previous month's figure was particularly strong, the end-December number will show a more moderate outturn by comparison.
Others believe end-December credit growth will accelerate at an even faster pace than in November, giving rise to further fears of overheating within the economy.
Economists' forecasts range from 15 to 17 percent for credit growth in the month of December from 16.4 percent at end-November.
At the top end of expectations, Riada economist Padhraic Garvey believes credit growth continued to rise in December and the outturn for the month will top November's rate.

"We are seeing a consumer boom and with that backdrop we are bracing ourselves for underlying credit growth rate of 17 percent year-on-year as the consumer and housing boom has continued unabated," Riada's Garvey said.
Economists at Davy and NCB stockbrokers are going for more conservative estimates.

"We don't expect the pace of growth to have picked up again on what was a very strong number the previous month," NCB senior economist Eunan King said. "We are still talking about 15 percent growth from 16.4 percent last time."
Davy stockbrokers economist Michael Crowley is pitching his estimate at 15.5 percent.

"The underlying trend is still upwards but it is not as marked as it was in November," Crowley said. "We are looking for a deceleration in the year-on-year growth rate in private sector credit in December and we have pencilled in 15.5 percent."

Crowley said to achieve a slowdown in private sector credit growth Ireland would have to have an increase in interest rates "...and that is unlikely to happen with the Irish currency so high within the ERM grid and with EMU in the offing".
NCB concur, saying there is no incentive for the overall pace of credit growth to slow down.
"We think it will continue to grow within the 14 to 16 percent range," NCB's King said.
He said about four percent of the growth rate is put down to the booming housing market "...which is simply driven by the pace of growth at which the labour force is rising".
King estimates 1997 economic growth at six percent in real terms and possibly eight percent in nominal terms.
"So even if credit growth is just keeping pace with the economy, growing at eight percent, and with the housing component you are talking about underlying growth of 12 percent."
Riada's Garvey said credit growth could go as high as 20 percent during the year.
"We know there is a consumer boom and there is a possibility that that would tempt up retail prices and consequently ratchet up CPI inflation. That is the risk," Garvey said.

"One implication of that is that the central bank in 1997 will be looking at underlying credit growing in the range of 15 to 20 percent and that level is quite worrying, particularly when you consider it set a credit growth target at nine percent a few years ago."
